# **CHAPTER ONE** **INTRODUCTION**

## **1.1 Background to the Study**

Climate change is already altering livelihoods, public health, infrastructure, water security, and food systems across Africa. The continent has contributed a small share of cumulative greenhouse gas emissions yet faces severe exposure and limited adaptation finance and infrastructure. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change reports that climate change has reduced agricultural productivity growth in Africa by 34 percent since 1961, more than in any other region (IPCC, 2022). This unequal distribution of causes, impacts, and capacity to respond makes climate change an educational and justice issue as well as an environmental one.

Kenya's recent climate record makes the problem immediate. The Kenya Meteorological Department reported that 2023 was then the warmest year in the national record and that floods affected more than 750,000 people. Its subsequent report identified 2024 as the country's hottest year on record (Kenya Meteorological Department, 2024, 2025). Nairobi's informal settlements face recurring flood exposure, drainage failures, water contamination, unsafe housing, and livelihood disruption. Research in Kibera and Mathare documents effects across physical health, mental health, household finances, water and food access, and neighbourhood safety (Balakrishnan et al., 2024). A survey of 963 Kibera households also found that effective flood adaptation depends on community participation and on combining household action with public infrastructure and policy (Mulligan et al., 2017).

Young people need practical knowledge that connects these local hazards with adaptation choices and with the unequal distribution of climate responsibility. UNESCO's global youth survey found that 70 percent of respondents either could not explain climate change, could explain only broad principles, or reported knowing nothing about it (UNESCO, 2022). At the same time, Kenya has a strong base for mobile delivery: the Communications Authority of Kenya recorded 44.8 million mobile broadband subscriptions and 41.5 million smartphones by December 2024 (Communications Authority of Kenya, 2025). These national counts do not prove equal access in Kibera or Ruaraka, but they support a mobile first approach that reduces data use and remains functional when connectivity is intermittent.

Traditional climate education is commonly delivered through classroom lessons, printed materials, public campaigns, or short workshops. These approaches can provide trusted information and interpersonal discussion, but they are difficult to revisit after the session and may not be tailored to the daily risks of a specific neighbourhood. Existing digital systems improve reach. ClimateScience provides short courses and quizzes, Earth Hero combines a carbon calculator with suggested actions, and NASA Climate Kids uses games and multimedia to explain climate science. Their primary emphasis, however, is global science, personal emissions reduction, or younger learners rather than bilingual, Nairobi specific adaptation and climate justice education (ClimateScience, 2024; Earth Hero, 2025; NASA, 2026).

This proposal therefore investigates an offline capable Progressive Web Application that presents short English and Kiswahili learning modules on urban flooding, heat, water stress, climate sensitive disease, unequal emissions, accountability, and safe civic participation. The software is not intended to forecast weather, replace formal teaching, or conduct campaigns. Its purpose is to make verified local knowledge easier to access, measure short term learning, and identify whether the design is usable enough to justify further development.

## **1.2 Statement of the Problem** 

Nairobi youth are exposed to climate hazards without consistent access to practical, locally grounded learning on how to prepare for and respond to them. Extreme weather affects health, income, water access, mobility, and education in informal settlements, while general climate curricula may stop at definitions and mitigation. UNESCO's findings on weak youth climate understanding and Nairobi evidence on multidimensional extreme weather impacts show an educational gap that is both measurable and consequential (Balakrishnan et al., 2024; UNESCO, 2022).

Available software does not adequately combine three requirements of this setting: Nairobi specific adaptation, climate justice literacy, and reliable use under intermittent connectivity. ClimateScience offers structured courses, Earth Hero emphasizes personal footprint reduction and action tracking, NASA Climate Kids targets younger learners, and the Kenya Meteorological Department portal provides authoritative forecasts and reports without a guided youth learning pathway. None of these systems was designed to test whether Nairobi youth improve both adaptation knowledge and justice awareness through a bilingual offline capable learning experience (ClimateScience, 2024; Earth Hero, 2025; Kenya Meteorological Department, 2024; NASA, 2026).

This study introduces a mobile first Progressive Web Application with reviewed English and Kiswahili modules, offline lesson access, low bandwidth media, quizzes, progress tracking, and verified civic learning resources. The application will be piloted with approximately 50 youth aged 15 to 24 in Kibera and Ruaraka. A one group pretest and posttest evaluation, usability survey, usage records, and focus group feedback will assess short term knowledge change, usability, engagement, and advocacy self efficacy. The pilot will not establish population wide effects or prove causality; it will determine whether the proposed solution is feasible and sufficiently promising for a larger controlled study.

## **1.3 Aim and Objectives of the Study**

The aim of this study is to design, develop, and evaluate an offline capable mobile first web application that improves access to locally relevant climate adaptation and climate justice education for youth in Nairobi.

### **1.3.1 Specific Objectives**

1\.  To identify the climate adaptation information needs, climate justice knowledge gaps, connectivity constraints, and content preferences of youth aged 15 to 24 in Kibera and Ruaraka through literature review and a focused needs assessment.

2\.  To design and develop a bilingual Progressive Web Application that delivers reviewed Nairobi specific learning modules, quizzes, progress tracking, verified resources, and offline access to core content.

3\.  To evaluate the pilot using defined learning, usability, engagement, and qualitative metrics, including pretest and posttest scores, System Usability Scale results, module completion, synchronisation success, and participant feedback.

## **1.4 Research Questions**

1\.  What climate adaptation information needs, climate justice knowledge gaps, and access constraints should guide the application design for youth in Kibera and Ruaraka?

2\.  How can a bilingual offline capable Progressive Web Application be designed to deliver locally relevant adaptation and climate justice education in a usable and accessible form?

3\.  What changes in knowledge and advocacy self efficacy, and what levels of usability and engagement, are observed during the pilot?

## **1.5 Project Scope**

**Geographical scope.** The pilot is limited to Kibera and Ruaraka in Nairobi County. The two locations provide different urban contexts but are not statistically representative of Nairobi or Kenya.

**Population scope.** The target group is approximately 50 youth aged 15 to 24, with an intended balance of about 25 participants per location. Recruitment will seek variation in gender and education status through cooperating community organisations or educational institutions.

**Content scope.** The initial release will contain seven core learning modules: climate change and Nairobi risk; urban flooding; heat and health; water stress and disease prevention; unequal emissions and climate justice; evaluating green claims; and safe civic participation and accountability.

**Technical scope.** The deliverable is a responsive Progressive Web Application for modern mobile and desktop browsers. Core lessons and saved progress will work offline after first access. The pilot will not include native Android or iOS applications, real time forecasting, artificial intelligence recommendations, financial transactions, open social networking, or direct petition and campaign tools.

**Research scope.** The evaluation measures immediate and short term outcomes during a sixteen week project. It does not measure long term behaviour, community resilience, reduced disaster losses, or policy change.

## **1.6 Significance and Justification**

The project will give pilot participants a reusable source of Nairobi specific adaptation guidance and climate justice education that can be accessed on a phone and revisited without continuous connectivity. Its bilingual, low bandwidth design addresses practical access barriers instead of assuming stable data and high end devices.

The study will produce evidence beyond software performance. Pretest and posttest results will show whether participants improve on adaptation and justice knowledge, while usability, completion, and qualitative feedback will show whether they can and want to use the product. This evidence will identify which content and design decisions deserve further investment.

The work also offers a replicable technical and evaluation model for community organisations and educators. Any decision to scale will remain conditional on the pilot findings, independent content review, safeguarding requirements, and a larger study capable of estimating effects more credibly.

## **1.9 Definition of Terms**

**Adaptation literacy.** The ability to identify climate hazards, interpret local risk information, and select feasible actions that reduce harm.

**Advocacy self efficacy.** A participant's confidence in finding credible information, communicating a concern, and using safe and lawful channels for civic participation.

**Climate justice.** An approach that examines how responsibility for emissions, exposure to harm, decision making power, and access to adaptation resources are distributed.

**Climate justice awareness.** Knowledge of unequal emissions and impacts, procedural fairness, responsibility, and credible accountability pathways.

**Offline capable.** Able to load previously cached lessons and save progress without an active connection, then synchronise eligible records when connectivity returns.

**Progressive Web Application.** A web application that uses browser capabilities such as a service worker, a web app manifest, caching, and local storage to provide an installable and resilient experience.

**Youth.** For this project, people aged 15 to 24 who live or study in Kibera or Ruaraka.

# **CHAPTER TWO** **LITERATURE REVIEW**

## **2.1 Introduction**

This review sought software related and empirical literature on digital climate education, mobile learning, offline delivery, technology acceptance, climate literacy, climate justice, and urban adaptation in Nairobi. A structured narrative approach was used because the proposal must connect technical design evidence with social and educational evidence rather than estimate a single pooled effect. Searches were conducted across Google Scholar, PubMed, publisher databases, and institutional repositories using combinations of climate education, mobile learning, Nairobi youth, Kibera flooding, climate justice, offline learning, usability, and Progressive Web Application. The final evidence base contains 27 peer reviewed, government, intergovernmental, and primary technical sources selected for relevance, traceability, and methodological usefulness. Product claims were checked against official pages for the four existing systems reviewed below.

## **2.2 Conceptual Review**

The proposed intervention treats the quality of the learning application as the principal independent variable. Quality is represented by local relevance, language accessibility, interactivity, offline reliability, source transparency, and ease of use. Exposure is not reduced to account creation; it includes lesson access, quiz attempts, module completion, and successful recording of progress. These variables can be observed through usage records and participant responses.

The primary dependent variables are adaptation literacy and climate justice awareness. Adaptation literacy covers recognition of local hazards and selection of appropriate actions. Climate justice awareness covers unequal responsibility and impacts, procedural fairness, and evidence based accountability. Advocacy self efficacy is a secondary outcome because knowledge alone may not translate into confidence to use credible, safe participation channels.

Perceived usefulness, ease of use, and engagement may mediate the relationship between the application and learning outcomes. Baseline knowledge, age group, education status, location, prior climate experience, device access, and connectivity may influence both exposure and outcomes. The pilot will describe these factors but will not have sufficient statistical power to estimate a complex mediation model.

![Figure 2.1 Conceptual framework][image3]

*Figure 2.1 Conceptual framework*

## **2.3 Historical Background of the Research Topic**

### **2.3.1 Origins and Early Context**

Climate education developed from environmental and science education that initially emphasised physical processes, conservation, and individual responsibility. As climate impacts became more visible, adaptation entered policy and education, particularly in countries facing immediate risks. Climate justice expanded the focus by asking who produced emissions, who receives protection and finance, whose knowledge counts, and who participates in decisions. This shift is important in Africa, where low historical emissions coexist with high exposure and adaptation constraints (IPCC, 2022).

Digital learning followed a separate path from desktop educational software to web platforms and mobile applications. Early systems depended on continuous connectivity and institution owned computers. Smartphone access and browser capabilities later made mobile learning more feasible, while service workers and local databases allowed web applications to cache resources and queue data. The educational value still depends on the learning design; delivery technology does not compensate for generic content, poor scaffolding, or weak assessment.

### **2.3.2 Key Milestones**

**2013 to 2014\.** Research consolidated evidence that adaptation is culturally embedded and that Africa faces serious climate vulnerability, shaping the case for locally grounded learning (Adger et al., 2013; Niang et al., 2014).

**2015 to 2017\.** Kenya's National Adaptation Plan defined national adaptation priorities, and community responsive flood research in Kibera demonstrated the value of combining local knowledge, household action, and public systems (Government of Kenya, 2016; Mulligan et al., 2017).

**2019 to 2022\.** Economic and climate assessments documented unequal impacts, while UNESCO's youth survey exposed major climate knowledge gaps. Mobile learning studies also showed that locally situated digital activities can support conceptual learning (Diffenbaugh & Burke, 2019; Mettis et al., 2022; UNESCO, 2022).

**2023 to 2025\.** Kenya updated its national climate action plan, Nairobi experienced severe climate extremes, and research documented multidimensional impacts in informal settlements. Mobile broadband and smartphone use continued to expand, strengthening the feasibility of mobile delivery without removing the need for offline design (Balakrishnan et al., 2024; Communications Authority of Kenya, 2025; Government of Kenya, 2023).

### **2.3.3 Historical Gaps and Transition to the Current Study**

The historical record reveals three persistent gaps. Climate information is often global rather than neighbourhood specific; education frequently separates adaptation from questions of responsibility and power; and software designed for broad reach may assume stable connectivity or offer limited evidence of learning. Research on Nairobi's informal settlements describes exposure and community adaptation, but it rarely evaluates a digital tool that combines adaptation and justice education for youth. The current study addresses that intersection while keeping its claim narrow: it tests feasibility and short term outcomes in two locations.

## **2.4 Theoretical Review**

### **2.4.1 Foundational Theories**

Constructivist learning theory provides the educational foundation. Learners build understanding by connecting new information to prior knowledge and lived experience. The proposed modules therefore begin with familiar Nairobi scenarios, ask learners to make choices, provide feedback, and connect general climate concepts to observable hazards. Mobile learning evidence supports contextual tasks that link scientific ideas to everyday settings (Mettis et al., 2022; Väljataga & Mettis, 2022).

The Technology Acceptance Model explains why a technically correct system may still fail. Davis (1989) identifies perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use as central determinants of acceptance. In this study, local relevance and actionable guidance should strengthen usefulness, while mobile first navigation, short modules, bilingual delivery, and offline access should reduce effort. The model informs usability questions but is not treated as proof that intention leads to sustained use.

Climate justice provides the substantive lens. It links distributive questions about impacts and resources with procedural questions about voice and decision making, as well as recognition of different histories and knowledge systems. The application will present evidence on unequal emissions and impacts alongside adaptation choices. Content will distinguish established findings, contested claims, and participant values so that justice education does not become partisan instruction.

Together, these theories form the study's theoretical framework. Constructivism guides scenario based learning, the Technology Acceptance Model guides usability and adoption measures, and climate justice guides content selection and interpretation. The framework predicts that locally meaningful content must also be easy to use and ethically presented before it can support learning and civic confidence.

## **2.5 Overview of Existing Systems**

Four software systems were reviewed because each addresses part of the proposed problem. ClimateScience offers short climate courses and quizzes. Earth Hero calculates a personal footprint and recommends actions. NASA Climate Kids presents accessible games, activities, videos, and articles. The Kenya Meteorological Department portal provides authoritative national forecasts, reports, and advisories. The comparison focuses on observable software functions and fit with the proposed users rather than on claims about product intent.

### **2.5.1 Strengths and Weaknesses of Existing Systems**

Table 2.1 Comparison of existing software systems

| System | Relevant functions | Strength | Gap for this study |
| ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| ClimateScience | Short courses, quizzes, levels, global climate topics | Structured and engaging learning pathway | Limited Nairobi specific adaptation and justice content; offline pilot fit not established |
| Earth Hero | Footprint calculator, goals, personalised actions, sharing | Turns information into trackable personal actions | Primary frame is personal emissions reduction; limited local adaptation instruction |
| NASA Climate Kids | Games, activities, videos, articles | Clear multimedia explanations from an authoritative science organisation | Designed mainly for younger learners and global science; no Nairobi pilot assessment pathway |
| KMD portal | Forecasts, advisories, reports, climate services | Authoritative Kenya specific climate information | Information portal rather than a guided bilingual youth curriculum with pretest and posttest evaluation |
| Proposed PWA | Local modules, offline access, bilingual content, assessments, progress and verified resources | Combines Nairobi adaptation, justice literacy, and research measurement | Small pilot, no long term evidence, and content quality depends on independent review |

The comparison does not establish that the proposed product is superior. It establishes a testable design gap: none of the reviewed systems combines the study's content, access, and measurement requirements. The pilot must show whether this combination produces usable learning rather than assuming that feature integration creates value.

## **2.6 Review of Related Works**

Empirical research supports the need for local context. Adger et al. (2013) show that culture shapes how people understand impacts and adaptation, while Mulligan et al. (2017) demonstrate in Kibera that community engagement affects the feasibility of flood responses. Balakrishnan et al. (2024) extend this local evidence by documenting how extreme weather affects health, finances, water, food, drainage, safety, and social life in Kibera and Mathare. These studies justify content based on lived urban conditions rather than generic lists of climate actions.

Research also supports the learning approach, although not in the same population. Mettis et al. (2022) used mobile outdoor learning with 158 secondary students and found gains in knowledge and conceptual change. Väljataga and Mettis (2022) similarly examined knowledge gain and scaffolding needs in mobile outdoor settings. These studies indicate that mobile technology can support contextual learning, but their designs and settings do not show that an offline web application will work for Nairobi youth. This proposal therefore measures learning directly.

The justice content rests on documented evidence rather than rhetorical attribution. Diffenbaugh and Burke (2019) found that historical warming increased economic inequality between countries. Supran et al. (2023) quantitatively assessed ExxonMobil's internal projections and found that most accurately forecast warming, while a joint congressional staff report documented continuing public communication practices designed to avoid accountability (United States House Committee on Oversight and Accountability & United States Senate Budget Committee, 2024). These sources support a module on evidence, responsibility, and evaluating claims. The module will present cited documents and avoid asserting legal liability that the study cannot determine.

For usability, the System Usability Scale provides a short standardised instrument suitable for a pilot (Brooke, 1996). A score of 68 is commonly treated as an approximate benchmark for average usability (Bangor et al., 2009), but the result will be interpreted with confidence intervals and qualitative comments rather than as a pass or fail verdict. The study will also record completion, error, and offline synchronisation rates because perceived usability alone cannot show whether the software works under real access conditions.

### **2.6.1 Summary of Reviewed Literature**

Table 2.2 Summary of empirical literature

| Source | Method and sample | Relevant finding | Design implication |
| ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| Adger et al. 2013 | Cross regional conceptual and empirical synthesis | Culture is integral to climate impacts and adaptation | Use local knowledge and avoid universalised content |
| Diffenbaugh and Burke 2019 | Econometric analysis of 165 countries | Warming increased between country economic inequality | Ground justice content in measurable distributional evidence |
| Mulligan et al. 2017 | Survey of 963 Kibera households plus stakeholder consultation | Community responsive approaches address limits of household and public action | Teach household actions together with collective and institutional responses |
| Mettis et al. 2022 | Action research with 158 learners | Mobile situated learning supported knowledge and conceptual change | Use contextual scenarios and measure learning before and after |
| Supran et al. 2023 | Quantitative analysis of company climate projections | Internal projections accurately forecast warming | Use primary evidence to teach claim evaluation and accountability |
| Balakrishnan et al. 2024 | Six monthly surveys with 800 women in Kibera and Mathare | Extreme weather effects span health, finance, services, safety, and environment | Represent climate risk as multidimensional and locally experienced |
| UNESCO 2022 | Global youth climate education survey | Large shares of youth reported limited ability to explain climate change | Assess baseline knowledge and design for explanation rather than exposure alone |

## **2.7 General Comments**

The literature supports the problem but does not guarantee the solution. Nairobi youth face real climate and information risks, locally situated mobile learning can support understanding, and digital access is sufficiently widespread to justify a mobile first experiment. However, direct evidence is missing at the intersection of Nairobi youth, adaptation literacy, climate justice, bilingual offline delivery, and measured learning outcomes. The proposed study addresses that narrow gap.

The evidence also places limits on the project. A 50 person purposive pilot cannot estimate effects for Nairobi's youth population, a one group design cannot separate the application effect from testing or maturation, and immediate posttest gains do not show long term behaviour change. These limits shape the methodology in Chapter Three and prevent promotional claims that the application has solved climate vulnerability.

# **CHAPTER THREE** **SYSTEM ANALYSIS AND DESIGN**

## **3.1 Introduction**

This chapter explains how the proposed application will be designed and how the pilot will be evaluated. The project uses a design science orientation because it creates and tests a software artefact in response to an identified problem (Hevner et al., 2004). A mixed methods pilot combines quantitative evidence from assessments, usability responses, and usage records with qualitative evidence from focus groups and observation (Creswell & Plano Clark, 2018). Agile development supports iterative implementation, while formal entry criteria separate software testing from research involving participants.

## **3.2 Research Design**

The evaluation uses a one group pretest and posttest pilot. Participants complete a baseline assessment, use the application during the defined pilot period, and complete an equivalent endline assessment and usability survey. Focus groups follow the quantitative stage to explain unexpected results and identify content or interaction problems. The design can estimate observed short term change within the pilot group but cannot demonstrate causality because it has no randomised comparison group.

Table 3.1 Research question and evidence alignment

| Research question | Evidence source | Analysis | Output |
| ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| RQ1 Needs and constraints | Literature review, short needs survey, stakeholder interview | Priority hazards, baseline gaps, language and connectivity needs | Requirements backlog and content plan |
| RQ2 Application design | Usability tasks, observation, technical verification | Task completion, SUS, accessibility and offline tests | Verified PWA prototype |
| RQ3 Pilot outcomes | Pretest and posttest, usage records, focus groups | Knowledge gain, self efficacy, completion, qualitative themes | Feasibility judgement and revision priorities |

### **3.2.1 Study Population and Sampling**

The target population is youth aged 15 to 24 who live or study in Kibera or Ruaraka. Approximately 50 participants will be recruited through cooperating community organisations or educational institutions, with an intended allocation of about 25 participants per location. Purposive quota sampling will seek variation by age group, gender, and education status. The sample is appropriate for a capstone feasibility pilot but is not statistically representative.

Eligible participants must fall within the age range, have regular access to a browser capable phone or a shared pilot device, understand English or Kiswahili, and complete the required consent process. Participants aged 15 to 17 must provide assent and have written parent or guardian consent. Participation in research will not be required to access public educational content after the pilot.

### **3.2.2 Data Collection and Analysis**

The needs assessment will use a short structured survey and up to four stakeholder interviews with youth facilitators, educators, or community organisation representatives. The baseline and endline assessments will contain 20 equivalent knowledge items, divided between adaptation literacy and climate justice awareness, plus five Likert items on advocacy self efficacy. Equivalent forms will use the same blueprint and difficulty rather than repeating every item verbatim.

After the intervention, participants will complete the ten item System Usability Scale and two open ended questions on the most useful and most difficult parts of the experience. Application records will capture coded participant ID, module access, completion percentage, quiz attempts, timestamps, and synchronisation status. They will not record free text messages, contact lists, precise location, or unrelated device activity.

Descriptive statistics will report means, medians, standard deviations, proportions, and 95 percent confidence intervals where appropriate. Paired knowledge scores will be analysed with a paired samples t test if difference scores are reasonably symmetric; otherwise, the Wilcoxon signed rank test will be used. Cohen's dz or a rank based effect size will accompany the significance test. Because this is a pilot, effect estimates and uncertainty matter more than a binary p value. Focus group notes will be analysed using a concise reflexive thematic process with an audit trail (Braun & Clarke, 2019).

Instrument quality will be addressed through a content review by at least one climate or environmental subject specialist and one education or youth practitioner. Five nonparticipant testers will complete cognitive interviews and usability tasks before the pilot. Internal consistency will be reported for multi item scales, but low reliability in a small sample will be treated as a signal to revise the instrument rather than concealed.

### **3.2.3 Software Development Life Cycle**

Development will follow six two-week Agile sprints informed by the Scrum Guide but adapted for a single developer (Schwaber & Sutherland, 2020). Sprint 1 covers requirements, ethics dependencies, and architecture. Sprint 2 delivers coded onboarding, language selection, and the assessment shell. Sprints 3 and 4 deliver modules, quizzes, progress, offline caching, and administration. Sprint 5 covers accessibility, security, performance, and external beta testing. Sprint 6 resolves blocking defects and prepares the pilot release. Pilot data collection begins only after consent materials, content review, and critical verification tests are complete.

### **3.2.4 Metrics for Evaluation**

Table 3.2 Evaluation metrics and decision rules

| Domain | Measure | Analysis | Decision rule |
| ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| Adaptation literacy | Ten scored items converted to 0 to 100 | Mean change and proportion gaining at least 10 points | Promising if at least 60 percent gain 10 or more points and mean change is positive |
| Climate justice awareness | Ten scored items converted to 0 to 100 | Mean change and proportion gaining at least 10 points | Promising if at least 60 percent gain 10 or more points and no item shows systematic misconception |
| Advocacy self efficacy | Five item Likert scale | Mean or median change with distribution | Interpret direction and uncertainty; no causal claim |
| Usability | System Usability Scale | Mean score and 95 percent confidence interval | Target mean at or above 68 with no recurring critical task failure |
| Engagement | Required module completion | Completed modules divided by assigned modules | Target at least 75 percent median completion |
| Offline reliability | Queued records and sync outcomes | Successful unique commits divided by eligible queued records | Target at least 95 percent without duplicate records |
| Accessibility and performance | Automated and manual checks on target devices | Critical WCAG issues, load and repeat access time | No critical blocker; cold load within 3 seconds on throttled 3G for the tested build |

The decision rules are pilot thresholds, not proof of effectiveness. If knowledge improves but usability or offline reliability fails, the product is not ready to scale. If usability is strong but learning does not improve, content and instructional design require revision before additional technical expansion.

## **3.3 System Analysis**

The system has two human roles: youth participant and administrator researcher. Public visitors may access general information, but research features require a coded participant account. The application separates educational content from research administration and stores only the data necessary to answer the research questions.

### **3.3.1 Functional Requirements of the System**

Table 3.3 Functional requirements

| ID | Requirement | Priority |
| ----- | ----- | :---: |
| FR01 | The system shall allow an authorised participant to create or activate a coded profile without entering a public display name. | Must |
| FR02 | The system shall present reviewed modules in English and Kiswahili with consistent lesson order and source links. | Must |
| FR03 | The system shall cache core lessons and application assets for offline access after first successful loading. | Must |
| FR04 | The system shall save quiz responses and progress locally when offline and synchronise them when connectivity returns. | Must |
| FR05 | The system shall administer baseline and endline assessments and store scored domain results. | Must |
| FR06 | The system shall show participants their module progress without exposing other participants' data. | Must |
| FR07 | The administrator shall manage reviewed content versions, participant access, and aggregate pilot status. | Must |
| FR08 | The administrator shall export a pseudonymous research dataset with a documented data dictionary. | Must |
| FR09 | The system shall provide verified links to official or established climate resources without hosting campaigns or public user posts. | Should |

### **3.3.2 Non Functional Requirements of the System**

Table 3.4 Non functional requirements

| Category | Measurable requirement |
| ----- | ----- |
| **Performance** | Largest Contentful Paint within three seconds on the defined throttled 3G test profile for the pilot build; cached lesson reopening within one second on tested devices. |
| **Accessibility** | Conform to WCAG 2.2 AA for pilot paths, including keyboard access, visible focus, text alternatives, contrast, labels, and zoom without loss of content (W3C, 2023). |
| **Security** | TLS in transit, strong password hashing for administrator accounts, short lived signed sessions, role checks, rate limiting, input validation, and no secrets in client code. |
| **Privacy** | Pseudonymous research IDs, separate consent records, no precise location, least privilege access, and documented retention and deletion dates. |
| **Reliability** | Core cached lessons remain readable offline; eligible queued records synchronise without duplicates; backup restoration is tested before the pilot. |
| **Compatibility** | Support the current and previous major versions of Chrome and Android WebView used on pilot devices, with graceful fallback on other modern browsers. |
| **Maintainability** | Typed interfaces, automated tests for scoring and sync logic, versioned migrations, a deployment guide, and a content review workflow. |
| **Availability** | Target at least 95 percent measured API availability during the monitored pilot, excluding planned maintenance; offline lessons remain available during outages. |

### **3.3.3 Proposed Model Diagram**

![Figure 3.1 Mission aligned design and evaluation model][image4]

*Figure 3.1 Mission aligned design and evaluation model*

The model links evidence and user needs to a co designed software artefact and then to measurable pilot outcomes. Results return to the backlog as prioritised changes. Consent, data minimisation, source review, accessibility, and the prohibition on in application campaigning operate as constraints throughout the cycle rather than as checks added after development.

## **3.4 System Design**

The system uses an offline capable three layer architecture. The client layer renders the user interface and maintains a local cache and synchronisation queue. The application layer validates requests, applies access rules, serves content, scores assessments, and produces authorised research exports. The data layer stores pseudonymous records, media assets, logs, and backups. This separation keeps offline behaviour explicit and prevents the administrator interface from being treated as part of the database layer.

![Figure 3.2 Progressive web application architecture][image5]

*Figure 3.2 Progressive web application architecture*

The use case model assigns each action to a human role. Automated behaviours such as scoring and caching are internal system responsibilities, not external actors. Youth users can study, complete assessments, and view their own progress. Administrators can manage reviewed content and participant access, monitor aggregate engagement, and export pseudonymous research data.

![Figure 3.3 System use case diagram][image6]

*Figure 3.3 System use case diagram*

The relational design separates participants, learning content, assessments, responses, and progress. Questions belong to the assessment bank rather than to an individual completed assessment. Responses connect an assessment instance to a question. A composite uniqueness rule on participant and module will prevent duplicate progress rows, while server generated idempotency keys will protect synchronisation from duplicate commits.

![Figure 3.4 Relational data model][image7]

*Figure 3.4 Relational data model*

The back end class design separates authentication, content, assessment, and progress rules into services. Repository classes isolate database access. Controllers remain thin and are omitted from the diagram because their role is limited to request validation, service calls, and response mapping. This structure is more maintainable than placing research scoring and persistence directly inside route handlers.

![Figure 3.5 Back end service and repository class diagram][image8]

*Figure 3.5 Back end service and repository class diagram*

The participant flow begins with information and consent, then creates a coded profile and captures baseline knowledge before module access. Participants repeat lessons until the required set is complete. Endline assessment and usability questions follow. The flow avoids algorithmic recommendations; the curriculum order is transparent and can be revised through content governance.

![Figure 3.6 Participant learning and assessment flow][image9]

*Figure 3.6 Participant learning and assessment flow*

Offline synchronisation uses a local queue with unique record identifiers. When the device reconnects, the service worker submits queued progress and quiz records to the API. The API validates the participant session and writes the records in a transaction. A committed identifier is returned so the client can mark the local item as synchronised. Failed items remain queued, and retries do not create duplicates.

![Figure 3.7 Offline progress synchronisation sequence][image10]

*Figure 3.7 Offline progress synchronisation sequence*

## **3.5 Development Tools**

Table 3.5 Development tools and rationale

| Layer | Proposed tool | Rationale |
| ----- | ----- | ----- |
| Interface | React with TypeScript and Vite | Component based mobile interface, static type checking, and efficient build tooling |
| Styling | Tailwind CSS | Consistent responsive layout and accessible design tokens |
| Offline layer | Service worker, Cache API, IndexedDB | Cached lessons, local progress queue, and controlled synchronisation |
| API | Node.js and Express | Small REST API with a mature package ecosystem and straightforward deployment |
| Database | PostgreSQL with Sequelize | Relational integrity for participants, assessments, responses, and progress |
| Security | TLS, signed sessions or JWT, bcrypt or Argon2, validation and rate limiting | Authentication, authorisation, transport protection, and abuse controls |
| Testing | Vitest or Jest, Supertest, Playwright, Lighthouse, axe | Unit, API, end to end, performance, and accessibility checks |
| Deployment | Vercel for the PWA and Railway or equivalent managed service for API and database | Pilot scale hosting with HTTPS, logs, and managed backups |
| Research analysis | R or Jamovi plus spreadsheet validation | Reproducible paired analysis, descriptive statistics, confidence intervals, and charts |
| Design and modelling | Figma and diagrams.net | Interface prototyping and editable system diagrams |

## **3.6 Ethical Considerations**

Ethics approval or written institutional clearance will be obtained before recruitment or data collection. Adults will provide informed consent. Participants aged 15 to 17 will provide assent and require separate written parent or guardian consent. Information sheets will describe the study purpose, activities, time, foreseeable discomfort, data use, voluntary participation, and contact route for questions in English and Kiswahili.

The software will minimise personal data. Research accounts will use coded identifiers; precise addresses, contact lists, public profiles, and open posting will not be collected. Consent records will be stored separately from research data. Access will be limited by role, exports will be pseudonymous, and the retention period and deletion procedure will be approved before the pilot. Participants may withdraw future participation, while the information sheet will explain any limit on deleting data that has already been anonymised and aggregated.

Climate impacts and injustice may cause distress, particularly for participants with direct experience of flooding or loss. Facilitators will allow participants to skip questions or stop without penalty and will provide locally appropriate support contacts approved by the partner organisation. The content will pair risk information with feasible protective actions and will not ask minors to join campaigns, contact political actors, or disclose personal experiences publicly.

The researcher supports climate justice as a project motivation. That position creates a risk of selecting only confirmatory evidence or framing contested issues as settled. Mitigation includes source logging, independent content review, neutral wording checks, balanced response options, disclosure of analytical decisions, reporting negative or null findings, and separation of education from political mobilisation.

The study provides direct educational access but will not offer payment for particular answers or completion outcomes. Refreshments and any transport support will be modest and described in advance. Recruitment through schools or community organisations will not allow teachers, managers, or facilitators to pressure participation or view individual responses.
